quickCheck.question: What does hygroscopic mean?
quickCheck.answer: Able to attract and absorb water from the surroundings.

book-399-4.questionInPlainEnglish: Which anticoagulant is in the usual lavender-top blood-count tube?
book-399-4.explanation: EDTA binds calcium, a mineral needed for blood clotting. Removing available calcium keeps the sample from clotting and helps preserve cells for a complete blood count.
optionExplanations: EDTA is the usual lavender-top additive.
Heparin is commonly used in green-top tubes.
Sodium citrate is commonly used in light-blue coagulation tubes.
Oxalate is associated with some gray-top tubes; it is not the lavender additive.

quickCheck.question: Why does binding calcium prevent a clot?

book-399-5.questionInPlainEnglish: What is the SI category for the seven fundamental measurement units?
book-399-5.explanation: Base units are the starting units of the International System of Units. Examples include meter for length, kilogram for mass, and second for time. Derived units combine base units, as speed combines meters and seconds.
optionExplanations: Base is the official category for the seven fundamental units.
Primary is not the SI category name asked for.
Derived units are built from base units.
Elemental is not the SI category for these seven units.
book-399-5.memory: Base units are the building blocks.

quickCheck.question: Is meters per second a base unit or a derived unit?

book-399-5.sourceNote: The rationale incorrectly lists katal as a base unit and counts eight quantities. The seven base units are second, meter, kilogram, ampere, kelvin, mole, and candela; katal is derived.

book-399-6.questionInPlainEnglish: Which factor does NOT enter the basic centrifugal-force relationship?
book-399-6.explanation: The question asks for the exception. Basic centrifugal force depends on mass, distance from the spinning center, and rotation speed. Temperature is not a direct term in that relationship, although it matters for sample preservation.
optionExplanations: Temperature is the exception: it is not directly in the force formula.
Mass affects absolute centrifugal force, so it is not the exception.
Speed strongly affects force; the speed term is squared.
Radius, the distance from the spinning center, affects force.
book-399-6.memory: Spin force uses mass, radius, and speed—not a temperature term.

quickCheck.question: Does relative centrifugal force require sample mass?
quickCheck.answer: No; RCF expresses acceleration relative to gravity.

book-399-6.sourceNote: Absolute force includes mass. RCF in ×g depends on radius and rpm, not mass; the stem uses the broader term centrifugal force.

book-399-7.questionInPlainEnglish: Which historical weight class is used to check an analytical balance?
book-399-7.explanation: A balance is checked with a weight whose mass is accurately known. In the older class system used by the book, Class S weights are the appropriate check for analytical balances.
optionExplanations: Class J is associated with microanalytical work in this older scheme.
Class M is a higher reference class for checking other weights.
Class P permits wider tolerances and is not the selected analytical check class.
Class S is the book’s analytical-balance calibration class.
book-399-7.memory: A known check weight tests the balance.

quickCheck.question: Why can an ordinary object not reliably calibrate a balance?
quickCheck.answer: Its true mass is not sufficiently known.

book-399-7.sourceNote: Class S is a historical designation. Current weight selection commonly uses ASTM or OIML classes matched to balance performance.

book-399-8.questionInPlainEnglish: What marking does the book associate with the pipette described?
book-399-8.explanation: The book selects two etched bands, a marking commonly associated with a blow-out pipette. Such a pipette needs its final liquid expelled as its instructions specify. Always read the actual pipette marking: TD means calibrated to deliver, not automatically blow out.
optionExplanations: Two bands identify the blow-out style intended by this question.
Self-draining capacity does not describe every delivery-calibrated pipette.
A dual-purpose label is not the identifying mark selected.
Blue graduation color is not a universal TD identifier.
book-399-8.memory: Two rings can mean blow out; TD alone does not.

quickCheck.question: Should every TD pipette be blown out?
quickCheck.answer: No; follow its calibration markings and instructions.

book-399-8.sourceNote: The source overgeneralizes: TD pipettes are not universally identified by two bands. Many TD volumetric pipettes drain by gravity and must not be blown out; the bands denote blow-out designs.

book-399-9.questionInPlainEnglish: Which apparatus keeps stored materials dry?
book-399-9.explanation: A desiccator is a sealed container with a drying agent beneath a shelf. The drying agent takes up moisture from the air inside, helping protect the stored chemical from water.
optionExplanations: A buret accurately dispenses liquid during titration.
A desiccator provides a dry enclosed environment.
A separatory funnel separates liquids that do not mix.
Vacuum means reduced pressure; by itself it is not the named dry-storage apparatus.

quickCheck.question: What is placed in a desiccator to absorb moisture?

book-399-10.questionInPlainEnglish: Which listed advantages does the book assign to a fixed-angle centrifuge?
book-399-10.explanation: A fixed-angle rotor holds tubes at a set slant inside a streamlined head. In the book’s comparison, less air resistance means less frictional heating and allows higher speeds. All three listed advantages follow that comparison.
optionExplanations: Less air friction is one stated advantage, but not the whole answer.
Less friction-related heating is also a stated advantage.
Higher operating speed is also a stated advantage in the comparison.
All three are intended benefits in the book’s rotor comparison.
book-399-10.memory: Less air drag can mean less heat and more speed.

quickCheck.question: What stays fixed in a fixed-angle rotor?
quickCheck.answer: The angle of the tubes relative to the spinning axis.

book-399-10.sourceNote: Actual safe speed and heating depend on rotor design, instrument limits, load, and cooling; fixed-angle geometry alone does not guarantee higher speed.

book-399-12.questionInPlainEnglish: Which instrument checks how fast a centrifuge rotates?
book-399-12.explanation: A tachometer measures rotation rate, usually in revolutions per minute, or rpm. Checking rpm helps verify that a centrifuge can provide the intended separation conditions.
optionExplanations: A tachometer measures rotational speed.
A wiper is not a rotation-measuring device.
A potentiometer measures or adjusts electrical potential-related quantities.
An ergometer measures physical work or exercise output.

quickCheck.question: What does rpm mean?

book-399-12.sourceNote: The three-month interval is the book’s schedule; use current manufacturer and laboratory maintenance requirements.

book-399-13.questionInPlainEnglish: Which balance counters a sample’s weight using electromagnetic force?
book-399-13.explanation: An electronic analytical balance uses an electromagnetic force to balance the load on its pan. The instrument converts the balancing signal into the displayed mass.
optionExplanations: A trip balance does not name this electromagnetic electronic design.
Class A is not the balance type defined by this mechanism.
Class S refers to a historical calibration-weight class, not this balance mechanism.
An electronic balance uses electromagnetic force compensation.
book-399-13.memory: Electronic balance: electricity balances the load.

quickCheck.question: What does the instrument counterbalance?
quickCheck.answer: The downward force from the material on its pan.

book-399-14.questionInPlainEnglish: Which listed tube top commonly identifies a serum-separator gel tube?
book-399-14.explanation: A serum-separator tube contains gel that moves during centrifugation to form a barrier between serum and the clot. The speckled, or tiger-top, design is the book’s listed example.
optionExplanations: Light blue commonly indicates citrate for coagulation testing.
Gray commonly contains a glycolysis inhibitor, often with an anticoagulant.
Lavender commonly contains EDTA for cell counts.
A speckled top is a common serum-separator gel tube.
book-399-14.memory: Tiger top traps serum above gel.

quickCheck.question: What does separator gel separate?
quickCheck.answer: Serum from the clot and blood cells.

book-399-14.sourceNote: Tube colors vary by manufacturer; verify the label and additive rather than relying on color alone.

book-399-15.questionInPlainEnglish: Which listed sequence is the correct blood-tube order of draw?
book-399-15.explanation: Blood cultures or other sterile specimens come first, followed by citrate light-blue tubes and then serum tubes. The order reduces contamination by organisms or by additives carried from one tube to the next.
optionExplanations: Sterile specimen → light blue → plain red is the correct sequence listed.
Putting the sterile specimen after blue and red increases contamination risk.
Drawing EDTA lavender before blue and red risks additive carryover.
Green before a sterile specimen is not the correct order listed.

quickCheck.question: Why is order of draw important?
quickCheck.answer: It helps prevent contamination and additive carryover.

book-399-15.sourceNote: Follow the current collection procedure for the specific tube system; the trailing section-title text is an OCR artifact.

book-399-16.questionInPlainEnglish: What is the name for adding all values and dividing by how many values there are?
book-399-16.explanation: The arithmetic mean is the familiar average. For 2, 4, and 6: add to get 12, then divide by 3 values to get a mean of 4.
optionExplanations: Median is the middle value after sorting.
Mode is the most frequent value.
Arithmetic mean is sum divided by number of values.
Geometric mean multiplies values and takes a root, rather than simply averaging their sum.
book-399-16.memory: Mean: add, then divide by the count.

quickCheck.question: What is the arithmetic mean of 5 and 9?

book-399-17.questionInPlainEnglish: Calculate percent CV when the mean is 89 mg/dL and two standard deviations equal 14 mg/dL.
book-399-17.explanation: Coefficient of variation, or CV, expresses scatter as a percentage of the mean. First find one SD: 14 ÷ 2 = 7 mg/dL. Then CV = (7 mg/dL ÷ 89 mg/dL) × 100 = 7.865%, rounded to 7.9%.
optionExplanations: 7.8% is below the correctly rounded value.
7.9% is correct: one SD is 7 mg/dL, and (7/89) × 100 = 7.865%, rounded to 7.9%.
15.7% is about twice the correct CV because one SD is only 7 mg/dL.
15.8% is also about twice the correct CV.
book-399-17.memory: CV uses one SD, even if the stem gives two.

quickCheck.question: What units does percent CV retain from mg/dL?

book-399-18.questionInPlainEnglish: How does the book recommend collecting data for a new Levey–Jennings control chart?
book-399-18.explanation: A Levey–Jennings chart plots control results over time around a mean and standard-deviation lines. Data from about 20 days include ordinary day-to-day variation; many repeats on one day miss that variation.
optionExplanations: Testing over 20 consecutive days gives the intended spread of routine conditions.
A single batch mostly captures within-run variation, not day-to-day changes.
Using only one person needlessly excludes operator variation from routine conditions.
Weekly testing for one month provides too few observations.
book-399-18.memory: To chart daily variation, gather data across days.

quickCheck.question: Why not use 20 measurements from one batch alone?

book-399-19.questionInPlainEnglish: What should happen first when a batch fails quality control?
book-399-19.explanation: Do not treat patient numbers as trustworthy until the control failure is investigated. Follow the test’s written out-of-control procedure, which gives a planned sequence for identifying and correcting the problem.
optionExplanations: Reporting first can release unreliable patient results.
Following the specified failure procedure is the appropriate first action.
Changing calibrator lots immediately may miss the actual problem and introduce another change.
Changing reagent lots immediately is also premature without the prescribed investigation.
book-399-19.memory: Control failure → stop release → follow procedure.

quickCheck.question: Can a failing control simply be ignored if patient results look normal?

book-399-20.questionInPlainEnglish: Which rule system is commonly used with Levey–Jennings charts?
book-399-20.explanation: Westgard multirules examine patterns such as a result beyond three SD or repeated results beyond two SD on the same side. They help distinguish random scatter from evidence of an analytical problem.
optionExplanations: Westgard multirules are the intended companion rules.
Cusum tracks cumulative deviations and is another monitoring approach, rather than the answer selected here.
Linear regression studies a relationship between variables.
A Youden plot compares paired control results, often across laboratories.
book-399-20.memory: Westgard adds rules to the control chart.

quickCheck.question: Why inspect a pattern rather than only one control value?
quickCheck.answer: Repeated small deviations can reveal a problem.

book-399-22.questionInPlainEnglish: How often would a normally distributed control exceed the upper two-SD limit by chance?
book-399-22.explanation: About 95.45% of normal values lie within ±2 SD, leaving 4.55% outside. Half that is above +2 SD: 2.275%, often rounded to 2.5%. That is about 1 in 40. The question asks only the upper tail.
optionExplanations: 1 in 10 is 10%, much more frequent than the upper-tail probability.
1 in 20 is 5%, closer to both tails combined than the upper tail alone.
1 in 40 is 2.5%, the intended approximate upper-tail rate.
1 in 100 is 1%, below the normal upper-two-SD rate.
book-399-22.memory: Two-SD outside has two tails; one tail is about 2.5%.

quickCheck.question: Does this question count results below the lower limit too?
quickCheck.answer: No; only results greater than 2.6 ng/mL.

book-399-23.questionInPlainEnglish: What comparison does a Youden plot display?
book-399-23.explanation: A Youden plot places each laboratory’s low-control result on one axis and high-control result on the other. Laboratories that are high on both may share a consistent positive bias; the paired pattern helps distinguish types of error.
optionExplanations: Paired low and high results from several labs are the intended use.
One control followed through time is more like a Levey–Jennings chart.
Comparing two methods on one specimen is a method-comparison task, not this definition.
Following two controls in one lab over time is not the interlaboratory use asked for.
book-399-23.memory: Youden pairs two controls from each lab.

quickCheck.question: What can both controls being high suggest?

book-399-24.questionInPlainEnglish: Which two control targets check gentamicin near both its trough and peak levels?
book-399-24.explanation: A trough is the low drug level before a dose; a peak is the high level after dosing. Controls should cover clinically important low and high concentrations. Here 1.5 µg/mL is below 2, and 6 µg/mL lies in the 5–8 peak range.
optionExplanations: 1 and 2 µg/mL are both low and do not test the peak range.
1 and 3 µg/mL still do not include the 5–8 peak range.
1.5 and 6 µg/mL cover both important regions.
5 and 6 µg/mL cover the peak area but miss the low trough level.
book-399-24.memory: Drug QC should check the valley and the mountain.

quickCheck.question: What is a trough level?
quickCheck.answer: The low drug concentration, usually measured just before the next dose.

book-399-25.questionInPlainEnglish: Which item does the book exclude from its direct laboratory quality-assessment measures?
book-399-25.explanation: The question asks for the exception. Specimen identification, analytical accuracy, and instrument maintenance directly monitor the testing process. The book classifies staff scheduling as an administrative task instead.
optionExplanations: Staff scheduling is the administrative exception chosen by the book.
Specimen collection and identity are major quality measures.
Accuracy and precision directly assess measurement quality.
Preventive maintenance protects instrument performance and belongs in quality assessment.
book-399-25.memory: Track the sample, the measurement, and the equipment.

quickCheck.question: Is checking patient identification part of quality assessment?

book-399-25.sourceNote: This is a narrow older classification. Modern quality-management systems can include staffing adequacy and scheduling because they affect quality.

book-399-26.questionInPlainEnglish: Which control-chart finding most clearly requires corrective action?
book-399-26.explanation: A result beyond three standard deviations is unusually far from the expected center. It triggers the commonly used 1₃s rejection rule. Patient results should be held while the cause is addressed.
optionExplanations: Alternating values within ±1 SD can be normal scatter.
Alternating within ±2 SD is not by itself the stated rejection pattern.
One value between 2 and 3 SD may be a warning rather than an automatic rejection.
One result outside ±3 SD meets the 1₃s rejection rule.
book-399-26.memory: Three SD out: investigate before release.

quickCheck.question: What does SD describe?
quickCheck.answer: How widely values scatter around their mean.

book-399-27.questionInPlainEnglish: Which change does the book identify as a possible cause of a sudden control-chart shift?
book-399-27.explanation: A shift is an abrupt move to a new average, rather than a gradual drift. Replacing a spectrophotometer lamp can change its light output and therefore measured signals, especially if checks or calibration are incomplete.
optionExplanations: Recalibration is intended to maintain agreement, though an incorrect recalibration can also create a shift.
A changed aspiration probe can also affect results; it is not the book’s selected example.
Changing the light source can abruptly change optical readings and is the selected answer.
Different technique by personnel can sometimes affect results, but is not the selected hardware example.
book-399-27.memory: Shift = sudden step; trend = gradual slope.

quickCheck.question: How does a shift differ from a trend?
quickCheck.answer: A shift is abrupt; a trend develops progressively.

book-399-27.sourceNote: The options are not exclusive: probe replacement, faulty recalibration, or operator changes can also cause shifts. The book’s lamp-change answer is retained.

book-399-28.questionInPlainEnglish: Which statistic measures the spread of a normal distribution in the original units?
book-399-28.explanation: Standard deviation, or SD, describes how far values typically spread around the mean. A small SD means values cluster tightly; a large SD means they are more scattered.
optionExplanations: Median identifies a central value, not scatter.
Mode identifies the most frequent value.
CV expresses SD relative to the mean as a percentage.
Standard deviation directly measures scatter around the mean in the measurement units.

quickCheck.question: Which has tighter clustering: SD 1 mg/dL or SD 8 mg/dL?

book-399-29.questionInPlainEnglish: Which term means the proportion of people without disease correctly testing negative?
book-399-29.explanation: Specificity asks about people who truly do not have the disease. It is true negatives divided by all people without disease: TN/(TN + FP). High specificity means few false alarms.
optionExplanations: Sensitivity asks how many diseased people test positive.
Specificity asks how many non-diseased people test negative.
Positive predictive value starts with people who tested positive.
Negative predictive value starts with people who tested negative, rather than all non-diseased people.

quickCheck.question: What is the denominator for specificity?

book-399-30.questionInPlainEnglish: What is unpredictable measurement scatter called?
book-399-30.explanation: Random error makes repeated results vary unpredictably above or below the underlying value. It is like repeated throws scattering around a target; it reduces precision.
optionExplanations: Random error is the unpredictable variation described.
Standard error of the mean describes uncertainty in an estimated mean.
Parametric analysis is a type of statistical method, not a measurement error.
Nonparametric analysis is another statistical approach, not the error named here.

quickCheck.question: Does random error mainly harm precision or create a fixed bias?

book-399-32.questionInPlainEnglish: Which term describes agreement with the true value?
book-399-32.explanation: Accuracy means closeness to the accepted true value. Precision means repeated measurements agree with one another. A tightly grouped set can still be inaccurate if the whole group is off target.
optionExplanations: Random error is unpredictable variation, not closeness to truth.
Precision is repeatability between measurements.
Accuracy is agreement with the true or reference value.
Variance quantifies spread and does not define truth agreement.
book-399-32.memory: Accuracy hits the target; precision groups the shots.

quickCheck.question: Can results be precise but inaccurate?
quickCheck.answer: Yes; they can cluster around the wrong value.

book-399-33.questionInPlainEnglish: What fraction of a normal distribution falls within two SD of the mean?
book-399-33.explanation: For a bell-shaped normal distribution, about 68.26% lies within one SD, 95.45% within two, and 99.74% within three. The question asks for the middle two-SD region.
optionExplanations: 34.13% is about the region from the mean to one SD on one side.
68.26% is the full ±1 SD region.
95.45% is correct because it is the central area within two standard deviations on both sides of a normal-distribution mean.
99.74% is approximately the ±3 SD region.

quickCheck.question: About what percentage lies outside ±2 SD?

book-399-34.questionInPlainEnglish: Which statistic does the book choose as a measure of dispersion?
book-399-34.explanation: Variance is the average squared spread around the mean, using the appropriate population or sample divisor. Squaring means large departures contribute strongly. It is one formal measure of how widely results scatter.
optionExplanations: Range also measures spread, using only highest minus lowest, so the wording is broad.
Validity describes whether a method serves its intended purpose, not a spread statistic.
Variance is the book’s intended measure based on squared deviations.
CV also measures relative spread as a percentage, making the general wording ambiguous.

quickCheck.question: How is standard deviation related to variance?
quickCheck.answer: Standard deviation is the square root of variance.

book-399-34.sourceNote: The question is not exclusive: range and coefficient of variation also measure dispersion. Variance is retained as the book answer.

book-399-35.questionInPlainEnglish: Which term means a method keeps both accuracy and precision over time?
book-399-35.explanation: Reliability means the method continues to produce trustworthy measurements during ordinary ongoing use. It needs both closeness to the right value and consistent repeat results.
optionExplanations: Reliability is sustained accurate, precise performance.
Validity concerns whether the method is appropriate for its purpose, rather than the specific ongoing-performance term.
Probability is how likely an event is.
Sensitivity concerns detecting disease or a small analytical change, depending on context.
book-399-35.memory: Reliable means right and repeatable over time.

quickCheck.question: Is repeatability alone enough for reliability here?
quickCheck.answer: No; accuracy must also be maintained.

book-399-36.questionInPlainEnglish: What statistic is calculated by the damaged formula in the source?
book-399-36.explanation: The book identifies the formula as sample variance: s² = Σ(x − mean)²/(n − 1). Subtract the mean from each value, square each difference, add the squares, then divide by one less than the number of values.
optionExplanations: CV is SD divided by the mean, usually multiplied by 100.
Variance is the mean squared-deviation calculation with n − 1 for a sample.
Confidence limits need an estimate plus or minus an uncertainty term.
Standard deviation is the square root of this variance expression.
book-399-36.memory: Squared differences without a final square root give variance.

quickCheck.question: What final step turns variance into standard deviation?

book-399-36.sourceNote: The stem formula is badly OCR-damaged. This explanation reconstructs the sample-variance expression implied by the book answer; verify the page image if the displayed formula differs.

book-399-37.questionInPlainEnglish: Which statement is NOT true about assayed quality-control material?
book-399-37.explanation: Assayed controls have assigned target concentrations and check whether a system is behaving. Calibrators set the system’s measurement scale. Using the same material interchangeably for both purposes can hide errors instead of independently detecting them.
optionExplanations: Resemblance to patient samples is a desirable control property.
Assigned analyte concentrations define assayed controls.
Interchanging controls and calibrators is the incorrect statement and therefore the answer.
Including normal and abnormal levels helps check performance across important ranges.

quickCheck.question: Why keep control and calibration roles separate?
quickCheck.answer: A check should independently detect an incorrect measurement scale.

book-399-38.questionInPlainEnglish: Which quality measure tracks how long results take to reach clinicians?
book-399-38.explanation: Turnaround time is the interval between defined workflow points, such as collection and result reporting. When urgent results arrive too slowly, tracking this time helps locate delays.
optionExplanations: Separation and aliquoting are steps that can cause delay, not the overall time measure.
Test utilization asks whether tests are being ordered appropriately.
Analytical methodology concerns how the test is performed.
Turnaround time directly measures speed of result delivery.

quickCheck.question: What does stat mean in a laboratory request?

book-399-39.questionInPlainEnglish: Which organization offers the external proficiency survey named here?
book-399-39.explanation: The College of American Pathologists, or CAP, provides proficiency-testing surveys. Laboratories test unknown samples and compare performance with assigned targets or peer groups, creating an outside check on internal control.
optionExplanations: CLSI develops laboratory standards and guidance, rather than being the survey answer here.
ASCLS is a professional organization, not the named survey program.
ASCP is a professional and certification organization, not the selected provider.
CAP is a major proficiency-testing survey provider.
book-399-39.memory: CAP surveys compare performance beyond one lab.

quickCheck.question: Why add external proficiency testing to internal controls?
quickCheck.answer: It provides an independent check of performance.

book-399-41.questionInPlainEnglish: What should be done when the morning control is beyond three SD?
book-399-41.explanation: Hold the affected patient results and investigate equipment, reagents, and the process. After correcting the cause, repeat the affected testing as required and verify acceptable controls before releasing reliable results.
optionExplanations: Releasing immediately ignores a significant control failure.
Repeating only until a control happens to pass can conceal a real error.
Investigating, correcting, and repeating affected work with acceptable controls is the proper course.
Calling repeated failure random error does not justify releasing results.
book-399-41.memory: Do not repeat until lucky; find the cause.

quickCheck.question: When may affected patient results be released?
quickCheck.answer: After the problem is resolved and required checks show acceptable performance.

book-399-41.sourceNote: Exact repeat scope and release criteria follow the validated out-of-control procedure; a result inside ±2 SD alone does not always establish full acceptability.

book-399-42.questionInPlainEnglish: What pattern triggers the Westgard 2₂s rule?
book-399-42.explanation: Two consecutive control results beyond the same two-SD boundary suggest a consistent shift. Both must be above +2 SD or both below −2 SD. Opposite sides indicate a different pattern.
optionExplanations: Results inside ±2 SD do not meet this rule.
One beyond +2 and one beyond −2 is not same-side 2₂s.
Two consecutive points outside the same +2 or −2 boundary give the full rule.
Two above +2 SD are one valid example, but this wording omits the equally valid low-side case.
book-399-42.memory: Two-two-s: two results, two SD, same side.

quickCheck.question: Do one high and one low result meet 2₂s?
quickCheck.answer: No; they must cross the same side’s limit.

book-399-42.sourceNote: The final option is a true subset of the full rule; the book selects the complete two-sided definition.

book-399-44.questionInPlainEnglish: What should be checked after a patient’s bilirubin jumps from 2.0 to 6.2 mg/dL despite acceptable controls?
book-399-44.explanation: A delta check compares the current result with the same patient’s earlier result. The rise is 6.2 − 2.0 = 4.2 mg/dL. Good controls do not rule out a mislabeled sample or other patient-specific problem, so investigate if the change exceeds the laboratory’s limits.
optionExplanations: Calling immediately without checking the surprising change may transmit an unverified result.
Sending straight to the chart skips the needed patient-specific check.
Repeating every patient’s run is not justified just by one unusual change.
A delta check and targeted investigation address the specific discrepancy.
book-399-44.memory: Good QC checks the system; a delta check checks the patient’s change.

quickCheck.question: Can good controls prove a sample belongs to the right patient?

book-399-45.questionInPlainEnglish: What is an error that consistently pushes measurements in one direction called?
book-399-45.explanation: Systematic error causes a repeated bias, such as results tending too high. It may be a fixed offset or grow with concentration. The question does not give enough detail to choose either subtype.
optionExplanations: Systematic error is the general term for a consistent directional bias.
Random error produces unpredictable scatter rather than one-direction bias.
Constant systematic error is specifically a fixed-size offset; that detail is not given.
Proportional systematic error grows with concentration; that detail is not given.

quickCheck.question: What extra clue would identify proportional bias?
quickCheck.answer: The size of the error increases with concentration.

book-399-46.questionInPlainEnglish: How many reference individuals are preferred for establishing a new reference interval by the usual nonparametric method?
book-399-46.explanation: A reference interval describes the expected spread in a defined reference population. At least 120 suitable individuals per group allows the usual nonparametric approach to estimate the central 95% without assuming a perfect bell curve.
optionExplanations: 30 is too few for the usual 120-person nonparametric establishment approach.
50 is also below the preferred count.
75 is below the usual minimum for this approach.
120 is the preferred minimum listed.
book-399-46.memory: Establish with 120; verify can use fewer.

quickCheck.question: Does a reference interval describe every healthy person with certainty?
quickCheck.answer: No; a typical central 95% interval leaves some healthy results outside.

book-399-47.questionInPlainEnglish: What does the book recommend after 4 of 20 results fall outside a proposed reference interval?
book-399-47.explanation: A small study may verify an existing reference interval rather than create a new one. Four outside is too many for immediate acceptance. The book recommends a fresh group of 20; accept if no more than two of that group are outside.
optionExplanations: Deleting results because they disagree would bias the study.
Using all 20 to create a simple ±2 SD interval does not follow the stated verification procedure.
Replacing only the four outside results selects a favorable answer rather than a fair new sample.
A new set of 20 provides the book’s independent second verification step.
book-399-47.memory: Do not erase disagreements; verify with a new group.

quickCheck.question: Why is deleting the four results inappropriate?
quickCheck.answer: It forces the data to match the desired interval.

book-399-47.sourceNote: This describes verification of a transferred interval, not full establishment; use current reference-interval guidance and assess participant suitability and outliers.

book-399-48.questionInPlainEnglish: Which item is NOT needed to calculate positive predictive value from test characteristics?
book-399-48.explanation: Positive predictive value is the chance a positive result represents true disease. It depends on sensitivity, specificity, and how common the disease is in the tested population. Precision is repeatability and is not a separate term in this calculation.
optionExplanations: Sensitivity affects the number of true positives.
Specificity affects the number of false positives.
Disease prevalence changes the balance of true and false positives.
Precision is the exception; it is not needed separately in the predictive-value formula.
book-399-48.memory: A positive’s meaning depends on how common the disease is.

quickCheck.question: Can the same test have a lower PPV in a low-prevalence population?

book-399-49.questionInPlainEnglish: Which counts are needed to calculate test sensitivity?
book-399-49.explanation: Sensitivity asks how many truly diseased people test positive. Add true positives and false negatives to count all diseased people. Sensitivity = TP/(TP + FN), usually multiplied by 100%.
optionExplanations: True positives and false negatives give the required numerator and diseased denominator.
True negatives and false positives are used for specificity.
True positives and false positives are used for positive predictive value.
True negatives and false negatives are used for negative predictive value.
book-399-49.memory: Sensitivity starts with everyone who really has disease.

quickCheck.question: If 90 diseased people test positive and 10 test negative, what is sensitivity?

book-399-50.questionInPlainEnglish: Calculate specificity when 45 of 50 people without malignancy test negative.
book-399-50.explanation: Specificity is the fraction of non-diseased people correctly testing negative. Here true negatives = 45 and total non-diseased = 50. Specificity = 45/50 × 100 = 90%. The other five are false positives.
optionExplanations: 10% is the false-positive fraction, 5/50, rather than specificity.
11% does not match the correctly negative fraction of 45 out of 50 people, which is 90%.
90% is the correctly negative fraction.
100% would require all 50 to test negative.

quickCheck.question: How many false positives occurred?

book-399-51.questionInPlainEnglish: Which counts calculate the chance that a negative result truly means no disease?
book-399-51.explanation: Negative predictive value starts with everyone who tested negative. Some are true negatives and some are false negatives. NPV = TN/(TN + FN), expressed as a percentage.
optionExplanations: True negatives and false negatives provide the needed counts.
True positives and false positives calculate positive predictive value.
True positives and false negatives calculate sensitivity.
True negatives and false positives calculate specificity.
book-399-51.memory: NPV asks: among negative tests, who is truly well?

quickCheck.question: Does NPV’s denominator include positive test results?
quickCheck.answer: No; it includes all negative test results.

book-399-52.questionInPlainEnglish: Which statement about proficiency testing is FALSE?
book-399-52.explanation: Proficiency-test samples are intentionally unknown so a lab’s routine performance can be assessed independently. Labs do not receive target acceptance ranges with the samples to decide whether to keep retesting for a passing result.
optionExplanations: Required proficiency testing is part of CLIA regulation for covered testing; this is broadly true.
CAP and the American Association of Bioanalysts are recognized providers; this is true.
Providers periodically send unknown samples; this is true.
Supplying acceptance ranges up front is the false statement and therefore the answer.
book-399-52.memory: Proficiency testing is an unknown challenge.

quickCheck.question: Why are the sample target values withheld?
quickCheck.answer: To evaluate ordinary performance without adjusting results toward the answer.

book-399-52.sourceNote: Requirements depend on test category and applicable regulations; the trailing “Laboratory Safety” is section-heading OCR text.

book-399-53.questionInPlainEnglish: Which chemical can become sensitive to a knock or shock after long storage?
book-399-53.explanation: Picric acid can become dangerously explosive when it dries or forms certain metal salts. The question points to this storage-related shock hazard. A suspect container requires the laboratory’s specialist hazardous-material procedure.
optionExplanations: Xylene is a flammable solvent, not the classic shock-sensitive solid described.
Picric acid can become shock-sensitive, especially when dry.
Chloroform has serious toxic hazards, but is not this classic shock-sensitive storage example.
Phenol is toxic and corrosive, rather than the specific answer here.
book-399-53.memory: Picric acid must not dry out.

quickCheck.question: What storage change makes picric acid especially concerning?
quickCheck.answer: Drying out or formation of sensitive metal salts.

book-399-54.questionInPlainEnglish: Which extinguisher classification is appropriate for energized electrical equipment?
book-399-54.explanation: In the US fire-class system, Class C means suitable for fires involving energized electrical equipment. The extinguishing agent must avoid conducting electricity back to the user.
optionExplanations: Class A covers ordinary solid combustibles such as paper and wood.
Class B covers flammable liquids.
Class C identifies suitability for energized electrical fires.
Class D is for combustible metals.
book-399-54.memory: C is for current in the US system.

quickCheck.question: Why is electrical suitability important?
quickCheck.answer: A conducting extinguishing agent could cause electric shock.

book-399-54.sourceNote: Fire-class lettering differs internationally; this question uses the US/NFPA classification.

book-399-55.questionInPlainEnglish: What hazard does the blue part of the NFPA diamond represent?
book-399-55.explanation: The NFPA hazard diamond uses colors to separate hazard types. Blue identifies health danger: how seriously exposure can harm a person. The number indicates severity within that system.
optionExplanations: Flammability is shown in the red section.
Health hazard is shown in blue.
Instability or reactivity is shown in yellow.
Contact is not the category assigned to blue.
book-399-55.memory: Blue = body/health; red = fire; yellow = instability.

quickCheck.question: Which NFPA color marks flammability?

book-399-56.questionInPlainEnglish: What hazard do xylene, ethanol, methanol, and acetone share?
book-399-56.explanation: These organic solvents can give off vapors that ignite. Their shared category in this question is flammable. Individual chemicals can have additional hazards too, such as toxicity.
optionExplanations: Corrosive means able to chemically damage tissue or materials; it is not the shared listed category.
Flammable fits their ability to form ignitable vapors.
Oxidizers promote combustion by supplying oxidizing power; these solvents are fuel instead.
Carcinogen is not the shared defining classification for all four.
book-399-56.memory: Solvent vapor can feed a flame.

quickCheck.question: Why can a solvent be a fire hazard before the liquid itself is hot?
quickCheck.answer: Its vapor can form an ignitable mixture with air.

book-399-57.questionInPlainEnglish: Which word means a substance can cause cancer?
book-399-57.explanation: A carcinogen can increase the risk of cancer. Cancer involves cells growing out of control. Other hazard terms describe different effects, though one chemical may have more than one type of hazard.
optionExplanations: A mutagen can change genetic material, which is not identical to proven cancer causation.
A teratogen can harm development before birth.
A carcinogen is a cancer-causing agent.
Reactive describes chemical instability or readiness to react, not specifically cancer.

quickCheck.question: What does teratogen refer to?
quickCheck.answer: An agent that can harm embryonic or fetal development.

book-399-58.questionInPlainEnglish: Which description best matches organisms handled at Biosafety Level 2 in this book?
book-399-58.explanation: BSL-2 is used for many agents that can cause human disease but present a moderate hazard when appropriate practices and equipment are used. The chosen description contrasts them with agents requiring higher containment for severe airborne or hard-to-treat disease.
optionExplanations: Agents not known to cause disease in healthy adults generally fit BSL-1.
Serious or lethal disease with available interventions more closely describes a higher-containment risk group.
Serious or lethal disease without available interventions points toward the highest containment risk group.
Human-disease agents with commonly available preventive or treatment measures best match the book’s BSL-2 description.
book-399-58.memory: BSL-2: moderate disease hazard, controlled work practices.

quickCheck.question: Does BSL-2 mean organisms are harmless?
quickCheck.answer: No; they can cause human disease.

book-399-58.sourceNote: The book’s “rarely serious” wording is simplified. Biosafety level is selected by agent- and procedure-specific risk assessment, not disease severity alone.

book-399-59.questionInPlainEnglish: What does a liquid’s flash point mean?
book-399-59.explanation: Flash point is the lowest temperature at which a liquid releases enough vapor to ignite briefly when an ignition source is applied under specified test conditions. It does not require the liquid to keep burning on its own.
optionExplanations: Self-sustained burning describes a different threshold, commonly the fire point, rather than flash point.
A maximum vapor pressure for spontaneous ignition is not the definition.
Enough vapor to form an ignitable mixture at the surface is the correct idea.
Flash point has no universal fixed relationship of 10°C above boiling point.
book-399-59.memory: Flash point: enough vapor for a flash.

quickCheck.question: Does flash point require a spark or flame in the test?
quickCheck.answer: Yes; it concerns ignition by an applied source.

book-399-61.questionInPlainEnglish: Which US agency enforces workplace safety and health laws?
book-399-61.explanation: The Occupational Safety and Health Administration, OSHA, sets and enforces workplace safety requirements. In laboratories these include rules addressing hazards such as chemicals and bloodborne pathogens.
optionExplanations: CAP accredits laboratories but is not the federal workplace-safety enforcement agency.
IATA develops air-transport rules, rather than enforcing US workplace safety law.
The Joint Commission accredits health-care organizations, not federal workplace legislation.
OSHA is the federal workplace safety and health agency.

quickCheck.question: What does occupational mean?

book-399-62.questionInPlainEnglish: Which term does the book use for an eight-hour chemical exposure limit?
book-399-62.explanation: A threshold limit value, or TLV, is an occupational exposure guideline. The time-weighted average version describes average exposure over a conventional eight-hour workday. It is not simply a highest allowed concentration at any instant.
optionExplanations: Flash point describes ignition conditions, not worker exposure.
HEPA describes particle filtration, not a chemical exposure concentration.
Threshold limit value is the intended exposure-guideline term.
A United Nations limit is not the occupational term selected here.

quickCheck.question: Is an eight-hour average the same as an instantaneous ceiling?

book-399-62.sourceNote: TLVs are ACGIH guidelines, not automatically legal maximums. OSHA permissible exposure limits are regulatory limits; short-term and ceiling limits also matter.

book-399-63.questionInPlainEnglish: Where does air from a conventional chemical fume hood go?
book-399-63.explanation: A conventional ducted chemical fume hood pulls hazardous vapors away from the worker and exhausts them outside through an appropriate building system. HEPA filters trap particles, but do not reliably remove chemical gases and vapors.
optionExplanations: Recirculating through HEPA alone does not remove many chemical vapors.
Exhaust outside the building is the conventional chemical-hood arrangement.
HEPA filtration is not the defining requirement for ordinary chemical-vapor exhaust.
A 30/70 recirculation split describes some biological-cabinet designs, not this chemical hood.

quickCheck.question: Why is HEPA alone inadequate for many chemical fumes?
quickCheck.answer: HEPA traps particles, while gases and vapors can pass through.

book-399-63.sourceNote: This refers to conventional ducted fume hoods. Specialized filtered ductless hoods exist only for assessed, compatible applications.

book-399-64.questionInPlainEnglish: Which airflow direction helps keep microbiology-room hazards away from offices?
book-399-64.explanation: Negative pressure means air flows into the laboratory from adjacent cleaner areas when a doorway is opened. This helps keep contaminated laboratory air from escaping into administrative spaces.
optionExplanations: Negative pressure directs air toward the laboratory, containing potential contamination.
Positive pressure pushes air out toward neighboring areas, the opposite containment direction.
Ignoring airflow removes an important containment consideration.
A HEPA filter alone does not define the necessary pressure direction.

quickCheck.question: In a negative-pressure room, which way does air move at the door?
quickCheck.answer: From the corridor into the room.

book-399-64.sourceNote: Pressure and filtration requirements depend on biosafety level, activities, and facility risk assessment; not every routine microbiology space has identical specifications.

book-399-65.questionInPlainEnglish: Which broad chemical hazard best fits the book’s extensive containment and decontamination precautions?
book-399-65.explanation: The book associates this set of precautions with carcinogens, substances that can cause cancer. A fume hood limits breathing exposure, suitable gloves reduce skin contact, and validated cleanup prevents carryover. The exact controls must match the chemical.
optionExplanations: Corrosives need protection too, but this is not the book’s intended overall hazard group.
Carcinogens are the intended category for this exposure-minimizing procedure.
Azides have particular toxic and explosive-salt hazards, not this general set’s selected answer.
Acids are corrosives, but are not the broader category selected here.
book-399-65.memory: Carcinogen controls minimize routes of exposure.

quickCheck.question: Why must glove material match the chemical?
quickCheck.answer: Some chemicals pass through or damage unsuitable gloves.

book-399-65.sourceNote: These precautions are not unique to carcinogens. Respirators and strong-acid/solvent decontamination are not universally required or appropriate; use the chemical-specific validated procedure.

book-399-66.questionInPlainEnglish: What should a laboratorian remove before going to lunch?
book-399-66.explanation: A lab coat can carry contamination from the work area. Remove it before entering eating areas and wash hands, so laboratory material is not carried to food or clean surfaces.
optionExplanations: Safety goggles are not the needed step for leaving to eat.
Removing the lab coat prevents carrying contamination into the lunch area.
Water alone is not an appropriate universal bench decontaminant.
Used gloves should be discarded appropriately, not saved in a coat pocket.
book-399-66.memory: Lab coat stays with lab work.

quickCheck.question: Should used disposable gloves be kept for reuse at lunch?

book-399-67.questionInPlainEnglish: Which listed action creates a biological hazard?
book-399-67.explanation: A used blood-collection needle can puncture a waste bag and injure anyone handling it. Sharps belong immediately in the designated puncture-resistant sharps container, not an ordinary wastebasket.
optionExplanations: Using standard precautions is protective practice, with added precautions when indicated.
Waiting for the centrifuge to stop before opening is protective.
Placing broken glass and other sharps in a suitable container prevents puncture injuries.
Discarding used needles in a patient’s wastebasket creates a needlestick hazard.
book-399-67.memory: Sharps go straight into sharps containers.

quickCheck.question: Who can be injured by a needle in ordinary trash?
quickCheck.answer: Anyone handling the trash, including cleaning and waste staff.

book-399-68.questionInPlainEnglish: Which listed chemical-storage practice is the acceptable one?
book-399-68.explanation: If flammable solvents require cooling, use equipment specifically designed for that hazard, in limited quantities and with compatible storage. Ordinary refrigerators can contain ignition sources that ignite accumulated vapor.
optionExplanations: Alphabetical storage alone can put incompatible chemicals beside each other.
A working fume hood is not a general storage cabinet for flammables.
Heavy liquid bottles on top shelves increase spill and injury risks.
A suitable explosion-protected refrigerator is the intended safe cold-storage choice.
book-399-68.memory: Cold flammables need a refrigerator designed for flammables.

quickCheck.question: Why is an ordinary household refrigerator unsuitable?
quickCheck.answer: Its electrical components may ignite solvent vapor.

book-399-68.sourceNote: Modern labels distinguish flammable-material storage refrigerators from explosion-proof models; choose equipment based on internal and surrounding hazards. Segregate chemicals by compatibility.

book-399-69.questionInPlainEnglish: What is the immediate response when concentrated acid covers someone’s lower body?
book-399-69.explanation: Get the person under the safety shower immediately and start abundant water flushing. Remove contaminated clothing while flushing as trained. Fast rinsing removes acid and limits continued tissue damage; arrange emergency help at the same time.
optionExplanations: Calling security alone delays the essential flushing.
The safety shower gives immediate large-volume rinsing and is the best first action.
Transporting first lets acid keep burning during the trip.
Adding concentrated base can produce heat and worsen the injury.
book-399-69.memory: Chemical on body: shower and flush immediately.

quickCheck.question: Why not neutralize acid on skin with concentrated base?
quickCheck.answer: The reaction can release heat and cause additional chemical injury.

book-399-70.questionInPlainEnglish: How should a bottle of corrosive reagent be carried to the hood?
book-399-70.explanation: Use a compatible bottle carrier with handles and secondary containment. If the primary bottle slips or breaks, the carrier helps contain the spill and protect the person carrying it.
optionExplanations: A suitable rubber carrier provides protection and secondary containment.
Pouring at the storage site may expose people outside the proper controlled work area.
Carrying an open, filled pipette risks a spill or exposure.
Supporting a bottle by hand gives less protection than a proper carrier if it breaks.

quickCheck.question: What does secondary containment do?
quickCheck.answer: It catches liquid if the main container leaks or breaks.

book-399-72.questionInPlainEnglish: Which occupational infection is the major hazard emphasized by this textbook?
book-399-72.explanation: The book emphasizes hepatitis, especially bloodborne hepatitis viruses, because clinical laboratories frequently handle human blood. Vaccination against hepatitis B and bloodborne-pathogen precautions greatly reduce risk.
optionExplanations: Tularemia can be a laboratory hazard but is not the broad blood-exposure answer here.
Salmonella can infect laboratory workers, but is not the book’s main answer.
Tuberculosis is an important airborne hazard, but the selected broad historical answer is hepatitis.
Hepatitis is the textbook’s major job-related disease hazard.

quickCheck.question: Which hepatitis infection has a routine protective vaccine?

book-399-72.sourceNote: The claim that hepatitis is the single major occupational disease hazard is historical and varies by laboratory activities, vaccination, and current epidemiology.

book-399-73.questionInPlainEnglish: Which role does the book assign to running and maintaining the laboratory safety program?
book-399-73.explanation: The laboratory safety officer coordinates the safety program, including procedures, training, and monitoring. Management still has overall responsibility for providing a safe workplace, and all workers must follow the program.
optionExplanations: A state public health laboratory does not run every clinical lab’s internal safety program.
A chemical hygiene officer focuses specifically on the chemical hygiene program.
The laboratory safety officer is the broad coordinating role selected.
The chief pathologist has leadership responsibilities, but is not the named operational role selected here.
book-399-73.memory: Safety officer coordinates the safety system.

quickCheck.question: Does a safety officer remove workers’ own safety responsibilities?

book-399-74.questionInPlainEnglish: What hazard can develop when azides build up as salts?
book-399-74.explanation: Azides can react with metals such as lead or copper in plumbing to form shock-sensitive metal azides. Accumulation can create an explosion hazard, so disposal must follow the laboratory’s approved chemical procedure.
optionExplanations: Explosive salt buildup is the specific concern.
Simple pipe corrosion is not the main azide-salt danger described.
Extreme volatility is not the main reason for monitoring salt accumulation.
Ordinary flammability near a flame is not this distinctive hazard.
book-399-74.memory: Azides plus plumbing metals can make explosive salts.

quickCheck.question: Why is drain disposal of azide-containing material concerning?
quickCheck.answer: It can form dangerous metal azides in plumbing.

book-399-75.questionInPlainEnglish: Which biological safety cabinet uses filtered downward airflow in the work area?
book-399-75.explanation: A Class II cabinet combines inward airflow at the front opening with HEPA-filtered downward airflow over the work area. It protects the worker, the environment, and the sample when used correctly.
optionExplanations: Class I protects personnel and environment but does not provide the same clean downflow product protection.
Class II uses the described filtered downflow.
Class III is a sealed glove-box style cabinet.
Class IV is not a standard biological safety cabinet class in this scheme.
book-399-75.memory: Class II: inward front air plus clean downflow.

quickCheck.question: What does HEPA filtration remove?

book-399-76.questionInPlainEnglish: What do Standard Precautions assume about human blood and potentially infectious material?
book-399-76.explanation: Treat human blood and other potentially infectious material as possible sources of infection regardless of a person’s apparent health or perceived risk. Infection is not always visible or already diagnosed.
optionExplanations: Assuming potential infectivity for every relevant specimen is the correct approach.
Waiting for proof of infection leaves unknown cases unprotected.
A respirator is not required for every blood specimen; PPE depends on exposure routes and tasks.
Intact skin does not remove risks to eyes, mouth, or from sharps.
book-399-76.memory: Precautions follow the exposure, not a guess about the person.

quickCheck.question: Can healthy-looking patients carry bloodborne infections?

book-399-76.sourceNote: Standard Precautions are broader than this bloodborne summary and include exposure-based practices for other body fluids, mucous membranes, and nonintact skin.

book-399-77.questionInPlainEnglish: What exhaust difference does the book emphasize between Class II A and B cabinets?
book-399-77.explanation: Many Class II Type A cabinets can return HEPA-filtered exhaust to the room, while Type B cabinets are ducted to exhaust outside. HEPA removes particles but not most chemical vapors, so cabinet subtype matters for chemical use.
optionExplanations: Type A may return HEPA-filtered exhaust to the room; this is the intended distinction.
Type B exhaust is directed outdoors, not simply returned to the room.
Size is not the defining distinction.
A gas jet is not a defining Type A feature and open flames can disrupt safe cabinet airflow.
book-399-77.memory: A may return air; B sends exhaust beyond the room.

quickCheck.question: Why does HEPA-filtered air not guarantee removal of toxic vapor?
quickCheck.answer: HEPA filters particles, not most gases or vapors.

book-399-77.sourceNote: Use current Class II A1/A2/B1/B2 specifications. Some Type A cabinets are canopy-connected to outdoor exhaust; configuration and permitted chemicals must be verified.

book-399-78.questionInPlainEnglish: What bleach dilution does this textbook recommend for blood-spill cleanup?
book-399-78.explanation: The book selects a 1:10 final dilution: one part household bleach plus nine parts water. That makes the stock one tenth as concentrated. For 100 mL total, use 10 mL bleach and 90 mL water, subject to the product’s validated instructions.
optionExplanations: 1:1 is undiluted stock in this final-volume notation and is stronger than the stated dilution.
1:10 is the book’s intended blood-spill dilution.
1:20 is half as strong as the stated 1:10 preparation.
1:100 is ten times more dilute than the stated preparation.
book-399-78.memory: One in ten total means one bleach plus nine water.

quickCheck.question: How much water joins 10 mL bleach for a 1:10 final dilution?

book-399-78.sourceNote: This is older generalized guidance. Required available chlorine, spill size, precleaning, contact time, and product instructions determine the current procedure; household bleach strengths vary.

book-399-79.questionInPlainEnglish: What should you do before using an unfamiliar disinfectant?
book-399-79.explanation: Read the manufacturer’s instructions and the approved laboratory procedure. The right concentration, surface contact time, and compatibility are essential; stronger is not automatically more effective or safer.
optionExplanations: Full strength may be inappropriate and could damage surfaces or increase exposure.
Reading and following the instructions gives the intended preparation and use conditions.
Increasing concentration by 10% is an unvalidated change.
Storing it under the sink does not establish correct use or safe compatible storage.
book-399-79.memory: Disinfection needs the right strength and the right time.

quickCheck.question: Why can a correctly diluted disinfectant still fail?
quickCheck.answer: The surface may not remain wet for the required contact time.

book-399-80.questionInPlainEnglish: Which written plan addresses exposure to bloodborne pathogens?
book-399-80.explanation: An exposure control plan describes how the workplace prevents and responds to bloodborne-pathogen exposure. It includes measures such as safe sharps handling, protective equipment, training, and post-exposure response.
optionExplanations: A chemical hygiene plan focuses on hazardous chemicals.
An exposure control plan is the specific bloodborne-pathogen plan.
Safety data sheets describe chemical hazards, not the full bloodborne control program.
An infection control plan is broader and is not the specific required plan name asked here.

quickCheck.question: Which plan covers laboratory chemical hazards?

book-399-80.sourceNote: “Material safety data sheets” is older terminology; current documents are called safety data sheets, or SDS.

book-399-82.questionInPlainEnglish: Which listed respiratory protection is appropriate for an assessed tuberculosis aerosol risk?
book-399-82.explanation: Tuberculosis can spread through tiny airborne particles. A properly selected and fit-tested N95 or higher-level particulate respirator filters inhaled particles. A loose surgical mask does not provide the same wearer protection.
optionExplanations: A carbon cartridge targets certain gases or vapors unless combined with a suitable particle filter; it is not the listed TB choice.
A loose mask is not equivalent to a fit-tested respirator.
Gloves protect hands but do not filter inhaled particles.
A fit-tested N95 particulate respirator is the intended answer.
book-399-82.memory: TB travels in air; protect breathing with a fitted respirator.

quickCheck.question: Why does respirator fit matter?
quickCheck.answer: Air can otherwise leak around the edges instead of passing through the filter.

book-399-82.sourceNote: The option conflates N95 and HEPA, which are different filter classifications. Respirator type and laboratory entry controls follow the assessed task, containment, and respiratory-protection program.

book-399-83.questionInPlainEnglish: What should determine which gloves are used with a chemical?
book-399-83.explanation: Choose gloves based on the chemical and the task, using compatibility and breakthrough-time information. A glove that stops one solvent may let another pass through even when it still looks intact.
optionExplanations: Chemical hazard and task determine suitable material, thickness, and duration of protection.
Transport distance alone does not tell whether a glove resists the chemical.
A fume hood reduces inhalation exposure but does not decide glove compatibility.
Availability alone is not a safe selection rule.
book-399-83.memory: Gloves need chemical compatibility, not just a good fit.

quickCheck.question: Can a glove look intact while a chemical passes through it?
quickCheck.answer: Yes; permeation can occur without visible damage.

book-399-84.questionInPlainEnglish: What maximum capacity defines the safety can asked about in this US laboratory question?
book-399-84.explanation: The book’s safety-can definition sets a maximum capacity of 5 US gallons, about 19 L. Such cans have features such as a self-closing lid and pressure relief appropriate to their approval; an ordinary large drum is not the same item.
optionExplanations: 1 gallon is within the limit, but is not the maximum.
5 gallons is the maximum capacity in this definition.
20 gallons exceeds the safety-can limit described.
55 gallons is a drum-sized capacity, far above this limit.
book-399-84.memory: Safety can: up to five gallons.

quickCheck.question: Is a 55-gallon drum the same as this defined safety can?

book-399-84.sourceNote: Capacity and construction requirements depend on the applicable jurisdiction and approval standard; this item uses the US definition of a safety can.
